title: How to make tutorial battle for RPG Maker MV

posts.author: Lumira
posts.body: Anyone please help me . I want to make tutorial battle for my game. The task at hand is to create a battle tutorial for new players in a game. The tutorial should restrict access to certain commands initially, gradually enabling them as the tutorial progresses. For instance, the first tutorial could involve facing two slimes and introducing the Attack command, while disabling other commands like Skill, Magic, and Guard. After explaining the purpose and functionality of the Attack command, players would then be required to use it to attack the enemies in order to unlock the other commands. The subsequent tutorials would follow a similar pattern, gradually introducing and enabling commands like Skill and Magic, as players progress through the tutorial. This approach ensures that players understand and learn each command one step at a time, enhancing their overall understanding and gameplay experience. Please help me to create the tutorial battle

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
First is, you need several tutorial states with seal traits for the skills you don't want to be enabled.
They should be without icon or messages as to hide them from the player during the tutorial.
That can disable everything but the item command. And the only thing you can do there is to not give the player any item before the tutorial.
Then you need special tutorial enemies and troops to give them detailed action patterns on which skill to use in which turn.
And lastly troop events for show text and perhaps force actions to guide the tutorial.

posts.author: redtide89
posts.body:
Sadly, a huge portion of players really hate tutorials. This could be for a variety of reasons, and you can speculate on those yourself.
What I can say is that I've had a life of watching friends start games that I love, that they often grow to enjoy and love as well, and I've been forced to watch them growl and grumble about even the smallest tutorial segment of a great game. This always stood out to me, because even as a kid, I often really enjoyed tutorials for games that I was interested in. So just keep some of that in mind --
1) As a kid, I actually liked the hand-holding, set-you-on-the-right-path-early style of tutorials really getting you off to the right start, especially for brutally difficult games. Doesn't matter what kind of game, could be Fire Emblem or League of Legends.
2) All of my friends were almost ubiquitously annoyed by tutorials. The same ones that piqued my interest would just give a completely different vibe to them. This behavior in turn annoyed me, but it's enough to take away that something about tutorials rubbed them the wrong way.
I should also mention that even those friends who played games less casually or had some obsessive nature (like me) in gaming would also appear to hate tutorials, but would put up with them as you'd expect.
Finally, and perhaps the only unique point I'll make here is that as I've grown older,
I've actually gained a hatred for certain types of tutorials in games that I feel actively damage my ability to learn the game that they are trying to teach me to play
-- at the time when I am trying my hardest to actively learn the game!
And this relatively new to me, not something that I've grown up with. This "thing" is when a tutorial locks you out of certain commands or controls in an attempt to railroad the player into something that the developer feels is "good" for them, such as understanding a common/intended way for a player to choose attacks or commands and progress through a battle.
What happens here is you take me, with all of my game knowledge that spans the years I've been alive playing games, likely similar ones to what I'm playing now, and going through a tutorial for a game that I'm mentally preparing myself to conquer and overcome. For the record, I tend to play games far more seriously than you'd expect, regardless of the actual difficulty or seriousness of the game. This is fun for me. So I
often find myself in a situation where the tutorial does more damage than good
, by locking out certain menu commands for me as I try to mentally map out all of the options available for future reference. Imagine thinking "okay, looks like I can only pick from these four options. Maybe pressing L or R does something? Nope, okay what about going back? Nope. Alright, now do I have to wait until I'm out of this tutorial to really test these buttons again? Because maybe the tutorial is just stopping me from accessing excess menus and information or commands."
Anyway, this kind of thinking makes me crazy, and it's entirely possible to write off something that is not exactly essential (think about nearly every Final Fantasy, which has extra buttons you can press for some niche effects that aren't needed for most players whatsoever, but if you know what they do then you can make use of them and it's fun to use the system to its fullest, especially when you can use it to your advantage to make up for part of the game that isn't as fun. Nearly every game has semi-undocumented features like this that you can take care of, but they aren't necessary to be told to the player, especially early on.
Imagine any of the Final Fantasy games. I'd argue that they would be slightly worse if the game stopped early on to tell you that you can do a few things to give you an advantage, like changing rows or defending instead of choosing Attack/Magic/Item for your turn. Yes, those commands are in the game and they might be self-explanatory for those of us who've been around the block, but adding them to a tutorial just bogs down the game ever so slightly, and further helps to not just ruin, but eliminate immersion. Furthermore, these commands are often overlooked because they have a niche use case, like Final Fantasy X's ability to change weapon mid-battle. The primary use is not so much to match an enemy weakness or add tedium to giving the player a moderately inconvenient way to add silencestrike to deal with magic-wielding enemies, but perhaps rather to manipulate the turn order, which is not something you can do as easily as in Final Fantasies 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, or 9. Perhaps even just never telling the player that they can do that would lead to the best experience. It's there if they figure it out on their own or come up with a use for it, and it's also easier to ignore if they can't figure out how to make use of it.
It probably makes more sense to remind the player that they could do those things later on in the game, not necessarily at any particular point in time, but an old-fashioned method is just having NPCs blurt battle mechanics at you in certain towns or pubs while the player is in "exploration" mode (and I mean both the player character and the brain of the human being behind the controls are in this "exploration" mode, and willing to find and take on new information piecemeal).
Anyway, I'm sure I've written too much already.
The sad part is that the developer has good intentions, but players derive pleasure from their games in many different ways. Some like to be told what to do, and others absolutely do not. Some like to figure out dominant strategies by themselves, and others would prefer to be told how to do it the right way from the beginning, so as not to "fall off" or "get behind" which they may have grown to fear from their own life's experiences. Still others might enjoy a more 'staircased' experience, learning large chunks of the game one at a time over the course of a playthrough.
Oh yeah, one more thing is that learning how to make a tutorial in your game might be more important than actually having the tutorial itself, because this knowledge lets you do more in the game itself. Like having scripted sequences in boss battles or something cool/interesting at times to keep the game fresh.
EDIT: Not that any of us are experts on this, but maybe 5-10 years ago it was popular game design theory to make sort of invisible tutorials, so the player doesn't realize they're actually inside of a tutorial and gets the best of both worlds (enjoying the game with training wheels temporarily, learning how to play and enjoy it better for when those guard rails are gone, and by the time they figure out they went through a tutorial it doesn't matter any more and the game is fun). There are also exceptions to this rule that take it a bit far, like many players perceiving Final Fantasy 13 to be approximately 30 hours of a tutorial. I'd argue that that much is still an enjoyable tutorial that truly lets you enjoy the game after that point for however much longer it lasts for you (provided you didn't pick easy mode... which probably should be called cinematic mode or something so players wouldn't mistakenly pick it and then walk away thinking that anyone can beat the game just pressing X).
